title: Greedy Sidon construction size lower bound

problemStatement.formal: theorem greedySidon_size_lower_bound (N : ℕ) (hN : N ≥ 1) : size (greedySidon N) ≥ Nat.sqrt N
problemStatement.plain: Prove that the greedy Sidon construction in {1,...,N} produces a set of size at least √N (or c√N for some explicit constant c > 0). This was previously stated as an axiom in Erdos156Problem.lean and subsequently removed. Formalizing the proof would close the gap.
whyMatters: Establishes a concrete lower bound on the greedy construction, complementing the maximality proof
The key counting argument (at step k, at most k² sums can block) is a standard technique worth formalizing
Combined with the Erdős-Turán upper bound, pins down the greedy Sidon set size to Θ(√N)

knownResults.goal: Prove the size lower bound |greedySidon(N)| ≥ c√N

currentState.focus: Initial creation as follow-up from erdos-156 completion
currentState.nextAction: Formalize the counting argument: at each step, the number of blocked elements grows quadratically in |A|

insights: Proof sketch: when |greedySidon k| = s, adding element k+1 is blocked iff ∃ a,b,c ∈ greedySidon(k) with a+k+1 = b+c. For each pair (b,c) there is at most one a, and for each a there are ≤ s choices of (b,c). So ≤ s² elements are blocked at size s.
Summing: total blocked ≤ Σ_{s=1}^{|A|} s² ≤ |A|³/3. Since we skip at most |A|³/3 of the N elements, |A|³ ≥ 3N so |A| ≥ (3N)^{1/3}. Wait, this gives N^{1/3} not √N.

Correction: the blocking count should be ≤ 2s-1 per step (each existing element a yields at most one blocking sum a+k=b+c). But actually: at step k with |A|=s, the number of values blocked is the number of x such that ∃ a∈A with x+a = b+c for some b,c∈A, i.e., x = b+c-a. There are at most s³ such triples but many repeat. More carefully: the number of sums in A+A is s(s+1)/2 (Sidon!), and for each sum σ and each a∈A, x=σ-a is blocked. So blocked count ≤ s·s(s+1)/2 ≈ s³/2. Over all steps, N ≤ s³/2, so s ≥ (2N)^{1/3}.

Actually the standard proof gives √N: at step N, if we haven't added k+1, then for A of size s, the sums a+(k+1) must hit an existing sum b+c. The number of existing sums is s(s+1)/2 ≤ N. Since each new element produces s new sums, and these must all be accounted for, the total sum space bounds s² ≤ 2N, giving s ≤ √(2N). But this is an UPPER bound on |A∩{1..N}|, not a lower bound.

The correct lower bound argument for greedy: element n+1 is rejected only if some pair in A gives a collision. The number of distinct sums in A+A is s(s+1)/2. The number of new sums created by adding n+1 is s (one for each a∈A: a+(n+1)). If any of these s new sums collides with the s(s+1)/2 existing ones, we reject. So we reject at most s(s+1)/2 elements before getting our (s+1)-th element. Total: N ≥ Σ_{s=0}^{|A|-1} 1 + ... ≈ |A|³/6, so |A| ≥ (6N)^{1/3}. This is N^{1/3}, not √N.

The √N bound for Sidon sets in {1,...,N} comes from the upper bound (Erdős-Turán), not the greedy construction. The greedy lower bound is Ω(N^{1/3}), which is the trivial bound for maximal Sidon sets.
nextSteps: Clarify the exact bound: greedy gives Ω(N^{1/3}), not Ω(√N)
